catalog_quote: [Krishnamurti 2003: 27, §1.5.1, family-wide] "The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each).The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A noninitial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants." [Bhaskara Rao 1972: 1-2, §1.1, transcribed from the page image] "The following is a list of segmental and suprasegmental phonemes of Kondekor Gadaba. ... Length : /:/ Nasalization : /~/ Intonation Features: Pitch Levels: /1/ Low, /2/ mid, and /3/ high. Terminal Contours : /|/ unmarked /||/ rising /N/ falling Transition Features: /+/ word juncture /, / clause juncture /#/ sentence juncture" [no stress phoneme; no stress/accent section in the chapter]

new_statements.quote: There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A noninitial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. §1.5 'Typological features of Dravidian', p. 27.
new_statements.locator: §1.5, p. 27 (PDF p. 30 of the on-disk chapter-1 file)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: extracted text of PDF p. 30 (book p. 27, section 1.5.1 Phonology) of gives, word for word: "There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A noninitial long vowel is louder than short vowels." The excerpt copy matches. The surrounding paragraph is a family-wide typological summary (vowel inventory, favoured syllable pattern, then the stress sentences, then the Proto-Dravidian consonant inventory); Gadaba is not named there. Reading fixed: initial syllable (non-phonemic, weight-insensitive, word-level) is what the sentence says, but it is a Dravidian default, not a Gadaba description; no…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide generalisation only: stress is non-phonemic and normally falls on the first syllable of the word regardless of its weight; a non-initial long vowel carries extra loudness. No Gadaba-specific statement was found: the accessible primary description (Bhaskara Rao 1972 thesis, phonology chapter) lists length, nasalization, pitch levels, terminal contours and junctures as the suprasegmentals and never mentions stress; Bhattacharya 1957 (Ollari) and Subba Rao 1992 are likewise silent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated at p. 27 (Steever 1998: 41 makes the same family-level claim with Konda as the noted exception).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('initial syllable of a word'), stated for Dravidian as a whole in a comparative handbook; it is not a description of Mudhili/Kondekor Gadaba and should be read as a family default, not a language-specific rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog mudh1235 'Mudhili Gadaba' = the Kondekor/Konekor/Salur Gadaba of Srikakulam-Vizianagaram districts, Andhra Pradesh (Bhaskara Rao 1972 preface: Panukuvalasa village near Salur, Srikakulam dt; PHOIBLE assigns his Konekar Gadaba inventory to mudh1235; Subba Rao 1992 describes the Vizianagaram-district variety). Bhattacharya 1957 'Ollari' describes the Koraput (Orissa) variety = Glottolog pott1240 Pottangi Ollar Gadaba, the sister language under the olla1234 Ollari-Gadaba node; Bhaskararao 1972 (citing Burrow & Bhattacharya 1962-63: 43) treats Ollari and Kondekor as one language with local differences. Not to be confused with Gutob/Bodo Gadaba (Munda, bodo1267), also spoken around Salur.

sources.note: Preface fixes the variety: informants from Panukuvalasa village near Salur, Srikakulam district, AP; speakers call themselves Kondekors; Ollari (Bhattacharya 1957) is the Koraput dialect, judged the same language with local differences (Burrow & Bhattacharya 1962-63: 43). Contents show the phonology chapter has no stress/accent section (only Length, Nasalization, Intonation features, Syllable).
